interpretation_rule: Lower ε* ⇒ more geometric privilege. Δ = ε*_tool − ε*_prose; positive Δ ⇒ privilege loss in tool mode. H1: mean Δ_safety > mean Δ_control.

hypotheses.detail: Tool-window ||h_L|| / prose ≈ 0.911. Relative blowup divides by ||h_L||, so a smaller tool norm biases ε* downward (negative Δ) for all directions. Magnitude (~9%) is smaller than the random mean shift and cannot alone explain why safety/learned mean Δ are positive while random is negative.

Near-threshold fixed-ε blowup ratios differ by direction type: task-aligned dirs (harmlessness/syntax) often show tool/prose relative-blowup < 1 (harder to blow in tool → positive Δ), while some orthogonal randoms show the opposite near τ. This is a real geometry difference, not only the pooled-mean artifact from averaging.

Original concern was tool mode globally more brittle (lower ε* / easier blowup for everyone). Random dirs move that way; safety/learned mean move the opposite way. So tool mode is not uniformly more brittle — orthogonal residual directions and task-aligned directions diverge. For 32B design: keep learned-control normalization primary; treat random mean Δ as a separate estimand (isotropic residual privilege), not as the H1 denominator.

random_delta_investigation.design_implication_32b: REQUIRED at 32B: (1) primary H1 = safety vs learned with BCa+joint transcript-cluster CI; (2) norm-matched relative and/or absolute blowup sensitivity to decompose random negative Δ; (3) report random mean Δ and ||h_L|| mode ratio as separate diagnostics.
random_delta_investigation.phrasing_note: Type×mode divergence redescribes the pattern and justifies keeping random as its own estimand; it is not a mechanism for why isotropic residuals gain privilege in tool mode. Mechanism remains open. Norm-matched / absolute blowup is a required 32B analysis, not optional.
